“Precisely the quality which makes him so intriguing,” replied my friend, holding the object of his scrutiny up to the lamplight. “Our client, Mr. Abernathy, who departed not an hour ago, left these spectacles upon the mantelpiece. He brought them here himself this morning, claiming a most peculiar tale of being shadowed in the street; a story the constabulary had dismissed as the fanciful notions of a man overwrought, but which struck me as having the ring of genuine terror.”

“And you mean to solve this grand mystery of a misplaced pair of spectacles?” I asked, with a touch of sarcasm.

“The spectacles are not the mystery, my dear Davies; they are the key,” he corrected me gently. “Mr. Abernathy will surely return for them. In the meantime, they may tell us something of the man we are to help. They are our only text.”

“Then what have you read? I see only a simple pair of spectacles, with steel frames and lenses thick enough to suggest a significant weakness of the eyes.”

“You see, but you do not observe. To the trained eye, these offer a veritable biography. For instance, it is plain that our Mr. Abernathy is a man of scholarly pursuits, most likely a botanist, who has recently travelled by sea. He is left-handed, possesses a nervous disposition, and while he is not a man of great wealth, he values quality and is prepared to pay for it. Most pressingly, however, his fears of being followed are not only justified; he is, I should say, in imminent peril.”

“Finch, you go too far!” I cried. “This is not deduction; it is fantasy. From a pair of spectacles?”

“It is a simple chain of reasoning. Here, take my lens and apply your own intelligence. What do you make of the minute residue upon the inner groove of the right lens?”

I took the spectacles and the proffered lens, and peered closely. “I see a speck of dust, perhaps. It is greenish in colour.”

“Exactly. And under high magnification, that speck reveals itself to be a particle of pollen from a species of orchid found only in the East Indies. Furthermore, here,” he pointed with the tip of a letter opener, “is a tiny stain, the result of a crushed leaf stem. Not the common detritus of a London park, I assure you. Ergo, a botanist, or at least a man who works closely with rare plants.”

“That is plausible enough,” I admitted. “But the sea voyage?”

“Observe the hinge. In the crevice, protected from any casual cleaning cloth, is a microscopic crystalline flake. It is salt, Davies, but not the coarse grain of the kitchen; it is the fine, misty deposit of sea spray. He has been on the ocean within the last few weeks, I should wager.”

“And his being left-handed?”

“A man who is right-handed will, when removing his spectacles, almost invariably grasp them by the left arm to pull them forward. A left-handed man does the reverse. The right arm of this pair is slightly smoother from more frequent handling, and, if you look very closely, you can see faint indentations upon the earpiece. The man has a habit of chewing upon them when he is thinking, and he brings them to his mouth with his dominant left hand.”

“Remarkable! And his financial state?”

“The frames are steel, not silver, and the design is purely functional. Yet look at this repair on the nose-bridge. It is not a clumsy solder, but a masterful piece of silver-smithing, almost invisible. A man of poor means would buy a new, cheap pair; a wealthy man would not have them repaired at all. Our client is a man of modest income who appreciates craftsmanship and prefers to maintain what he has. A man of some principle, I think.”

“But Finch, the danger! How could you possibly deduce that from a scratch on the glass?”

“Ah, that is the crux of it,” he said, his voice lowering. “Look at the left lens, just here. It is not a scuff, nor a crack from being dropped. It is a sharp, parabolic scratch. See how it arcs? This is the mark left by something sharp, a knife point I should think, which has been swiped across his face. He has flinched back at the last possible instant, and the blade, intended for his eye, has only grazed the glass. His pursuer is no mere shadow; he is a would-be assassin.”

“Good heavens, Finch!” I gasped, staring at the tiny flaw which now seemed a harbinger of death. “What are we to do?”

“We are to wait for Mr. Abernathy’s return. He now possesses something far more valuable than his spectacles; he has our undivided attention.”

As he spoke, the sharp ring of the street-door bell echoed up the stairs. Finch raised an eyebrow, a flicker of triumph in his eyes. “Sooner than I expected,” he murmured. “It appears the second act of our little drama is about to begin.” He gestured for me to remain silent as our landlady’s footsteps approached the door. A moment later, she entered, bearing a small silver tray.

“A telegram, Mr. Finch,” she said. “For a Mr. Davies.”

I took the envelope in astonishment and tore it open. My hands trembled as I read the terse message within. I looked up at Finch, my face pale.

“Well?” he asked, his posture suddenly rigid with anticipation.

“It is from the constabulary,” I stammered. “They have found a body in the botanical gardens at Kew. The man carried my card in his wallet. They ask if I can identify a Mr. Abernathy.”

The telegram, a flimsy yellow sheet, felt as heavy as a slab of granite. I stared at Finch, whose entire demeanour had transformed. The languid, intellectual curiosity had vanished, replaced by the sharp, predatory stillness of a hawk that has just spotted its quarry.

“Well, Davies?” he said again, his voice low and devoid of any of its earlier lightness. “The constabulary does not typically send for physicians to identify the departed unless there is some prior connection. The card, man, the card!”

“It is as I said,” I managed, my throat dry. “They have found a gentleman at Kew, and my professional card was in his wallet. They request my presence for an identification. They believe the man to be a Mr. Abernathy.”

Finch sprang to his feet in a single, fluid motion. He paced once across the hearthrug, his brow furrowed in intense concentration. “So, the wolf has caught the sheep,” he murmured, more to himself than to me. “The scratch upon the lens was not a warning; it was a failed attempt. The assassin was more determined, and more successful, than I had given him credit for. This is no longer a matter of deduction, Davies. It is a matter of retribution.”

He stopped and fixed me with a gaze of such intensity that I felt myself straighten in my chair. “There is no time to be lost. The police, with the best will in the world, will see only what is before their eyes. They will see a man, a wallet, a card. They will not see the parabolic scratch, the deposit of sea spray, or the masterful repair upon the nose-bridge. “But Finch,” I protested, “the hour is late, and the fog is setting in. Surely in the morning—”

“In the morning the trail will be as cold as Mr. Abernathy himself!” he snapped. “The killer believes he has what he came for. He may be making his escape from the city even as we speak. Every moment is precious. Come!”

There was no arguing with him in such a mood. I hastily pulled on my greatcoat, my mind reeling from the sudden and violent turn of events. Less than an hour ago, our greatest concern was the intellectual puzzle of a pair of spectacles; now, we were embroiled in a case of murder. As we descended the familiar seventeen steps to the street, I felt a knot of dread tighten in my stomach. Finch had deduced danger from a piece of glass, and his deduction had been proven tragically correct. What other dreadful truths lay waiting for us in the manicured gardens of Kew?

The journey was a grim and mostly silent one. We were fortunate enough to secure a hansom cab quickly, and as we clattered through the thickening London soup, the gas lamps swimming past us like hazy, indistinct spirits, Finch sat bolt upright, his chin upon his chest and his eyes closed. I knew, however, that he was not resting. His mind was racing, arranging and rearranging the few facts we possessed, seeking a pattern where I could see only chaos and tragedy.

“It is the why of it, Davies, that plagues me,” he said suddenly, without opening his eyes. “A common footpad does not stalk his victim. He strikes from the shadows, takes what he can, and flees. This was different. This was a pursuit. Abernathy was hunted. The first attack failed; the second, it seems, did not. The object of the chase must therefore be something of extraordinary value.”

“His money? A robbery, as the police will no doubt surmise?”

“No,” Finch said with certainty. “A man of his described means, a man who has his spectacles repaired rather than replaced, is not the sort to carry a fortune on his person. Besides, the nature of the first attack, a knife-thrust to the eye, is one of terror and precision, not the clumsy bludgeoning of a common thief. No, our assassin sought something Abernathy possessed, something he perhaps did not even know the value of. And our only clue to its nature is the sea spray.”

He fell silent again, and we rumbled on through the darkness until the gas lamps grew more sparse and the air took on the damp, earthy smell of the countryside. At length, the cab drew to a halt before the grand gates of the botanical gardens. A uniformed constable, his face ruddy in the lantern-light, stepped forward to intercept us.

“Police business,” Finch said, his tone sharp and authoritative. “I am Mr. Finch, and this is Dr. Davies. We are here at the request of the constabulary.”

The constable, evidently expecting us, nodded and led us through a smaller side-gate into the vast, shadowy expanse of the gardens. The fog was thicker here, swirling in ghostly eddies around the monolithic shapes of the great glasshouses, their curved roofs gleaming faintly in the gloom. Our guide led us down a winding gravel path, his lantern swinging rhythmically, casting long, dancing shadows that played tricks upon the eye. It seemed as though the exotic shrubs and trees were alive, whispering to one another as we passed.

Presently, we saw the glow of more lanterns ahead, clustered near the base of the magnificent Temperate House. A small group of men were gathered there, their dark forms silhouetted against the light. As we approached, one of them detached himself from the group and strode towards us. He was a stout, powerfully built man with a square jaw and a bristling, reddish moustache.

“Dr. Davies?” he inquired, his voice a low growl. “I am Inspector Wallace. I am grateful you could come at such short notice. A nasty business.”

“This is my associate, Mr. Finch,” I said, by way of introduction. “He has an interest in these small problems.”

Wallace gave Finch a cursory, slightly suspicious glance. “An amateur, eh? Well, there is little for an amateur to see here. It is a straightforward, if brutal, affair. The body is just over here. Be prepared, Doctor. It is not a pleasant sight.”

He led us to a canvas sheet laid upon the path. A constable lifted a corner, and I steeled myself. The man on the ground was indeed the same man I had seen in our rooms that afternoon. His face, which had been so animated with anxiety, was now a placid, waxy mask. His tweed jacket was dark with a spreading stain over the heart, and his sightless eyes stared up at the foggy sky. It was undeniably Mr. Abernathy.

“Yes,” I said quietly, a wave of sickness washing over me. “That is the man who called upon me today.”

“Robbery, plain and simple,” Wallace announced, with an air of finality. “His pockets have been turned out, and his wallet is gone, save for your card which was presumably dropped by the thief in his haste. While the Inspector was delivering his summary, Finch had dropped to one knee beside the body. He had produced his powerful lens and was ignoring the obvious, mortal wound entirely. Instead, he was minutely examining the victim’s right hand, which was loosely clenched into a fist. Wallace watched him with an expression of impatient disdain.

“There is nothing there, Mr. Finch,” the Inspector said. “We have already looked. The man fought for his life, no doubt, but he has nothing in his hand.”

“On the contrary, Inspector,” Finch murmured, without looking up. “He has everything. You see, but you do not observe.” With a pair of fine tweezers which he produced from a waistcoat pocket, Finch carefully worked at the dead man’s fingers. He extracted something so minuscule that it was all but invisible in the lantern-light. He placed it carefully into a small glassine envelope. “And his boots,” Finch continued, moving his attention to Abernathy’s feet. “You have noted the soil, of course?”

“It is a garden, Mr. Finch,” Wallace said, his patience wearing thin. “There is soil everywhere.”

“Indeed. But this is not the common, dark loam of these pathways. Look here,” he said, pointing with his tweezer. “This reddish, clay-like soil caked upon his heel. And here, in the tread. It is quite distinct. He has been somewhere else in the gardens before he met his end here.”

Finch stood up and swept his gaze around the immediate vicinity. He walked slowly over to a large, ornamental bush with broad, waxy leaves, not ten feet from the body. He bent low, his nose almost touching the gravel path.

“Ah,” he breathed. “And here are our other players. Two sets of footprints, Inspector, though the fog and the traffic of your own men have done much to obscure them. One is Abernathy’s, leading from the direction of the Palm House. The other… the other is most instructive.”

He pointed to a series of faint impressions in the damp gravel. “Our man Abernathy wears a standard English boot, size nine, with a worn heel. Our killer, however, wears a much narrower shoe, with a pointed toe and a distinctive diamond pattern on the sole. It is not an English make. French, I should venture, or perhaps Belgian. And see how deep the toe is pressed into the ground, and how shallow the heel? He was a man who walks upon the balls of his feet, a man of some agility. Furthermore, he waited here, behind this very bush. See how the gravel is scuffed? He was shifting his weight, impatient.”

Inspector Wallace stared from the faint marks on the ground to Finch’s face, a flicker of doubt warring with his professional pride. “That is all very well, Mr. Finch, but it is guesswork. A French shoe does not find me a murderer.”

“It is a starting point,” Finch replied coolly. “A better one than a missing wallet. The man you seek is not a common London cut-throat. He is a continental import, he is lithe, and he is patient. He did not kill for a handful of shillings. He killed for what Mr. Abernathy brought to this garden.”

Finch turned back to me. “Davies, did Abernathy mention what his purpose was in visiting Kew?”

“Only that he was a botanist,” I replied, my mind racing. “And that he had urgent business here. He seemed desperate to retrieve his spectacles, which he said were essential for his work.”

“Precisely. He needed to see something small, something that required close examination. And he came here. To the greatest collection of flora in the world. He was a botanist, recently returned from a sea voyage, with a peculiar reddish clay on his boots, and he was murdered by a foreigner for something he possessed.” Finch held up the tiny glassine envelope. Within it, a single, dark speck was visible. “I believe, gentlemen, that this is the key to the entire affair.”

Inspector Wallace squinted at the envelope. “What is it? A speck of dirt?”

“It is a seed, Inspector,” said Finch. “And I would wager my reputation that it is a seed unknown to science, or at least to the gardens of Europe. It is what Abernathy clutched in his dying moments. The killer took the wallet to create the illusion of a robbery, but he did not find this. This is what he was truly after.”

We left Inspector Wallace standing by the body, looking rather less certain of himself than he had been a few minutes prior. Our cab ride back to Baker Street was a different affair from the journey out. The fog seemed to be lifting, both outside and in my own mind, replaced by the electric excitement that always accompanied the unfolding of one of Finch’s cases.

“The clay, Finch, and the seed?” I asked, as we neared our lodgings.

“The resources of Kew are not merely its living plants, but also its library and its soil collections,” he explained. “There are glasshouses dedicated to specific climates, each with its own carefully prepared earth. The reddish clay on Abernathy’s boots will match the soil in one of those houses. That is where he went first. That is where he went to compare his prize, his single, precious seed, with the known specimens stored there. He confirmed its identity, or its novelty, and it was on his way from that place that he was intercepted.”

“And what is the seed?”

“Ah, that is the question that elevates this from a mere crime to a fascinating problem,” Finch said, a gleam in his eye as we drew up to our door. “Abernathy was a man of modest means, yet he undertook a sea voyage. He returned with something so valuable that a man would be sent from the continent to kill for it. A seed. What plant could possibly be worth a man’s life? A source of a potent new medicine? A flower of unimaginable beauty? Or perhaps,” his voice dropped, “the source of a poison for which there is no known antidote.”

He unlocked the door to 221B and strode into the sitting-room, shedding his coat. He went directly to his large chemical bench in the corner and, with the utmost care, tipped the contents of the glassine envelope onto a microscope slide.

“The first attack, Davies, was for the spectacles,” he mused, adjusting the focus. “The killer knew Abernathy carried his prize, but not where. He may have suspected it was in a locket, or a hollowed-out coin, or perhaps a secret compartment in the spectacle case itself. When that failed, he tracked him to the one place a botanist would go to verify such a treasure. He struck again, and this time he did not fail to kill his man. But he still failed to secure the prize.”

He fell silent, peering intently into the eyepiece of the microscope. The only sound was the hiss of the gaslight and the ticking of the mantelpiece clock. I waited, my own breathing seeming loud in the charged atmosphere.

“Good heavens,” Finch breathed at last, straightening up. His face was pale, and his eyes shone with a strange light.

“What is it, Finch? What have you found?”

“I have found our motive, Davies,” he said, his voice a near whisper. “I was wrong. It is not the seed of a new plant. It is not a seed at all.” He gestured for me to look.

I bent to the microscope and peered through the lens. There, on the slide, magnified a hundredfold, lay the dark speck. It was not the smooth, organic shape of a seed. It was an irregularly shaped, crystalline fragment, dark and lustrous. And embedded within its jagged surface, so small as to be invisible to the naked eye, was a minuscule fleck of brilliant, fiery red.

“A stone?” I said, perplexed. “A piece of grit?”

“It is a diamond, my dear fellow,” said Finch, his voice trembling with suppressed excitement. “An uncut, unpolished, industrial-grade diamond. But it is not from any known mine in Africa or India. The geology, the composition… and that tiny, scarlet inclusion. I have seen it described in only one text, a monograph on the mineralogy of the Guiana Highlands. This, Davies, is a fragment of a 'Tears of the Sun' diamond, so named for the red flecks within them. They are found in only one place on Earth, a single, inaccessible plateau in the deepest part of the Venezuelan jungle. A place from which, it is said, no man has ever returned.”

He began to pace the room again, his energy a palpable force. “It all makes sense! The sea voyage, the secrecy! Abernathy was no mere botanist. He was an explorer! He found it! He found the lost diamond field! He brought back a single, small sample as proof, disguised as a botanical specimen. But someone knew. Someone followed him. And they will stop at nothing to possess not just the sample, but the knowledge of its location.”

He stopped pacing and turned to me, his expression grim. “The killer did not find this stone. He will assume Abernathy had it hidden elsewhere. He will tear the man’s lodgings apart. He will search for maps, for journals, for any clue to the location. And that, my dear Davies, is where we are going next. For the hunter is now the hunted, and I am very much afraid that the game has only just begun.”

If he is not, then he may fear a trap, and our problem becomes a good deal more complex.” The commissionaire, his face still a mask of bewilderment, stammered his thanks and hurried from the room, leaving Holmes and myself to contemplate the magnificent jewel which now lay upon the plush of the tablecloth. It was a thing of rare beauty, its facets catching the winter light and casting a hundred tiny, dancing reflections upon the ceiling. Holmes, however, was not admiring its lustre. He was, as was his custom, lost in thought, his long fingers steepled before him, his gaze fixed upon the stone as though it were a crystal ball in which he could read the future. “You see, Watson,” he remarked at length, his voice low and thoughtful, “how easily I fall into old habits. My deductions concerning the hat were, in their own way, an amusing intellectual exercise. And yet, I pronounced the matter a ‘waste of energy.’ I dismissed it. Had Peterson’s wife not possessed an epicurean’s haste in preparing the goose for her table, this stone, this nexus of a great jewel robbery, would have been lost to us forever. It is yet another lesson, is it not? No problem is truly small. There are no trivial facts; there are only trivial observers.” He fell silent again, and for my part, I did not disturb him. The day wore on, the yellow London fog pressing in upon our windowpanes and lending an air of profound secrecy to the city outside. I watched my friend, whose mind was so clearly grappling with the fresh complexities of the case, and I reflected upon the change which had come over him in the past week. His recent errors, first in the matter of the Vance inheritance and now in his initial assessment of the lost goose, had not diminished his spirit. On the contrary, they seemed to have lit a new fire within him, a kind of fierce intellectual humility which made him more formidable than ever. It was as though he had been reminded that the world was not a mere logical puzzle to be solved from an armchair, but a living, breathing entity, full of passions and accidents which could overthrow the most perfect of syllogisms. At precisely half past six, there was a tentative knock upon our door. “He has come, Watson!” Holmes whispered, a thrill of anticipation in his voice. “If you would be so good as to show the gentleman in.” I opened the door to find a tall, stooping man of a somewhat scholarly appearance standing upon the landing. He was indeed middle-aged, with grizzled hair peeking out from beneath a borrowed-looking cap, and his face, though lined with worry, held a certain honest and kindly expression. He clutched a newspaper in one hand. “You are Mr. Henry Baker, I presume?” I enquired. “Yes, sir. I have come in answer to this advertisement,” he said, his voice a gentle rumble. “I can hardly believe my good fortune. I had quite given up all hope of ever seeing my hat again, to say nothing of the bird.” I led him into our sitting room, where Holmes rose to greet him, his manner a perfect blend of cordiality and keen scrutiny. “Mr. Baker, I believe?” said he. “Pray take a seat. I am Sherlock Holmes. It is a pleasure to make your acquaintance. Your property, I am happy to say, is quite safe.” He gestured to the sideboard, where the battered felt hat was resting. Our visitor gave a cry of delight and sprang forward to seize it. “My hat! My very own hat! Sir, I am deeply in your debt. I was set upon by a pack of ruffians, you see, and in the confusion, I fear I took to my heels with more haste than dignity.” “I can well imagine,” Holmes said smoothly. “The streets can be a perilous place. But there was the goose, as well. We were forced to consume it, I am afraid, as it showed signs of going off.” Mr. Baker laughed, a deep, hearty sound. “Oh, that is no matter, sir! No matter at all. I am just relieved to have my old hat. In fact,” he added, a twinkle in his eye, “I believe I owe your friend, the finder, a new goose for his trouble. I purchased it for my wife, you see, as part of a small club we have. Each of us contributes a few pence a week, and at Christmas we each receive a fine bird.” “An excellent arrangement,” Holmes remarked. “Well, Mr. Baker, as the goose is gone, we must return to you what is left of it.” He walked to the mantelpiece. “We found these in its crop. Its gizzard, I believe.” Holmes held out his hand, but instead of the brilliant blue diamond, he presented a few dull lead pellets. “The bird must have swallowed them at some point.” Mr. Baker peered at the pellets with mild curiosity. “Ah, yes. So it would seem. Well, it is of no consequence. Sirs, I cannot thank you enough for your trouble.” He clapped his old hat firmly upon his head and made to leave. “One moment, Mr. Baker,” Holmes said, his voice suddenly sharp as a razor’s edge. “Before you go, perhaps you could assist me with a small matter of academic interest. I have a theory about the rearing of geese, you see. Could you tell me where you procured your particular bird?” A look of utter bewilderment crossed Mr. Baker’s face. “Why, sir, I am not certain I can say. As I mentioned, it was from a club. The landlord of the Alpha Inn, near the Museum, he arranges it all. A most trustworthy fellow.” “I see. And you know nothing more of its origins?” “Nothing whatsoever, sir. And now, if you will excuse me, my wife will be growing anxious.” With a final nod of gratitude, he was gone, his footsteps echoing down the stairs. I turned to Holmes, my own mind in a whirl. “Holmes, what was all that about? The lead pellets? You still have the diamond!” “Precisely, Watson,” he said, a grim smile playing on his lips. “And I now know that Mr. Henry Baker, despite the evidence of his hat, has no more to do with the theft of the Blue Carbuncle than you or I. He is exactly what he appears to be: an honest, slightly down-at-heel gentleman who has lost his Christmas dinner. Had he shown the slightest flicker of recognition, the least hint of avarice or fear when I mentioned the contents of the crop, I would have known he was our man. But his ignorance was absolute, his relief at recovering his hat entirely genuine. He is not the thief, Watson. He is merely a signpost.” “A signpost? To what?” “To the Alpha Inn, my dear fellow. The goose began its journey there, and so shall we. The game, as they say, is afoot.” It was not long before we were wrapped in our coats and striding through the foggy streets towards Bloomsbury. The Alpha Inn was a public house of a common type, its windows glowing with a cheerless yellow light, its air thick with the competing odours of stale beer and cheap tobacco. Holmes, with his inimitable talent for assuming any character he chose, adopted the swagger of a man of the turf, and accosted the portly, red-faced landlord. “A wager, my good man!” he declared, slapping a sovereign down upon the sticky counter. “I’ll wager you a sovereign that the goose I bought from you last week was country-bred.” The landlord, whose name was Windigate, looked at him with suspicion. “And I’ll wager you a sovereign you’re talking nonsense. How would I know where the blessed things are bred?” “Come now,” Holmes cajoled, “you run a goose club. You must know your supplier. My bird won me a five-pound note, and my mate here,” he gestured to me, “disputes the fact. He says it was a common London bird.” The lure of a sovereign, and the appeal to his professional pride, was too much for the landlord. “Very well,” he grumbled, pocketing Holmes’s coin. “The birds come from a salesman in Covent Garden. A Mr. Breckinridge. And if you go and bother him, you can tell him that Windigate of the Alpha is tired of his noise.” “Breckinridge it is!” cried Holmes, with a triumphant wink in my direction. “Watson, we are another step along the chain!” Our next destination, the great market at Covent Garden, was a scene of controlled chaos. Even at this hour, porters hurried to and fro with crates of produce, their shouts echoing in the vaulted halls. We found Mr. Breckinridge, a horsey, aggressive-looking man with a temper as fiery as his waistcoat, presiding over a large stall. Holmes, changing his tactics, approached him with a business-like air. “Good evening. I believe you supplied some geese to the Alpha Inn recently?” Mr. Breckinridge scowled. “I supplied a couple of dozen. What of it?” “There has been a small mistake,” Holmes said, his voice low and confidential. “One of the geese, a fine bird with a black bar across its tail, was sold to the Alpha in error. It belonged to a Miss Oakshott, of Brixton Road, who is most anxious to have it back.” This approach, however, proved to be a miscalculation. Breckinridge flew into a rage. “I’ve had enough of your geese!” he bellowed, attracting the attention of several passers-by. “First that little rat pestering me about them, and now you! I sold the lot, and that’s the end of it. Be off with you!” But Holmes was not so easily deterred. The mention of another enquirer had sharpened his interest to a razor’s point. “A little rat, you say?” he asked, his voice calm in the face of the man’s fury. “Who was this other person?” “None of your business! Now, are you going to buy something, or are you going to stand there asking stupid questions all night?” At that moment, a small, pale man who had been loitering nearby, his face a picture of anxiety, scurried forward. “I say, Mr. Breckinridge,” he began in a reedy voice, “I just wanted to know for sure… about those geese from Miss Oakshott…” Breckinridge’s face turned purple. He seized a ledger from his counter and hurled it to the ground. “That’s it!” he roared. “I’m done! Here are my books! Find it yourself if you can, and devil take the lot of you!” He stormed off into the depths of the market, leaving the ledger lying in the dirt. Holmes moved with the speed of a striking cobra. He snatched up the book and drew the quaking little man into the relative quiet of a nearby alleyway. “I think, sir,” Holmes said, his eyes glittering, “that you and I have a great deal to discuss. My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other people don't know.” The man stared at him, his jaw agape. “You… you are not from the police?” “On the contrary. I am the one person who can keep you from them. Now, your name is John Robinson, is it not?” The man flinched as if he had been struck. “How could you possibly know that?” “I have been expecting you, or someone very like you,” Holmes replied, though I knew this to be a shot in the dark, designed to unnerve his quarry. “I know that you are a head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan, and that five days ago, a certain blue diamond went missing. A man named John Horner, a plumber, has been arrested for the crime. But he is innocent. The real thief, Mr. Robinson, stands before me now.” The man, whose true name we would soon learn was James Ryder, gave a strangled cry and collapsed against the grimy brickwork. His bravado, if he ever had any, evaporated in an instant, leaving only a pitiable, trembling wretch. “For God’s sake, Mr. Holmes, have mercy!” he whimpered. “It was my first slip, I swear it!” “Mercy is a commodity to be earned,” Holmes said sternly. “Take us to our rooms in Baker Street, and tell us everything. Your only hope of salvation lies in a full and frank confession.” And so it was that a short while later, the three of us were seated once more before the fire at 221B, the priceless gem lying between the terrified hotel attendant and the implacable amateur detective. Ryder, with much weeping and wringing of hands, told his squalid tale. He had learned of the diamond from the Countess’s maid, Catherine Cusack, and together they had conceived a plan to steal it and frame the plumber, Horner, who had a previous conviction. Ryder had taken the stone, but in a panic, and hearing footsteps approaching, he had fled the hotel. Desperate to hide the gem, he had gone to his sister’s house in Brixton, the very Mrs. Oakshott who raised geese for the London market. There, seeing a flock of birds in the yard, he had conceived of a desperate, foolish plan. He had seized the largest and most distinctive goose, prised its beak open, and forced the diamond down its throat, intending to retrieve it later. But when he returned, his sister informed him that she had sold the geese, and to his horror, he found that he had mixed up the birds. The one he had marked, a bird with a black bar on its tail, was still in the yard; the one containing the diamond had gone with the others to the dealer, Breckinridge. The rest was a frantic, hopeless chase, from his sister, to Breckinridge, to the Alpha Inn, always one step behind the fateful goose. When Holmes had heard him out, he stood and walked to the door. “The case is at an end,” he said quietly. “Get out.” Ryder stared at him, incredulous. “What, sir? Oh, heaven bless you!” “No more words. Be off!” Ryder scrambled to his feet and fled into the night, a man snatched from the very jaws of penal servitude. I turned to my friend in astonishment. “Holmes! You are letting him go? And what of Horner, the innocent man?” “Horner will be freed, Watson. Ryder’s disappearance will be the lynchpin in the collapse of the case against him. As for Ryder himself, he will not transgress again. He is too deeply terrified. If I send him to prison now, I may make him a hardened criminal for life. This way, I have saved a soul. Besides,” he added, a familiar twinkle returning to his eye, “it is Christmas, after all. And if one is to be humbled by one’s own fallibility, as I have been, it seems a poor time to be severe upon the fallibility of others. I have been reminded this week that appearances can be profoundly deceiving. The intellectual with the battered hat was a simple clerk. The small problem of a lost goose concealed a great crime. And the brazen thief proved to be a snivelling coward. It is a world of endless complexity, Watson, and I, for one, would not have it any other way.” He picked up his violin, and as the melancholy notes began to fill the fog-bound room, I knew that the lessons of the past week, the lessons of humility and the hidden depths of the seemingly trivial, had been well and truly learned. The game was more intricate than ever, and my friend was more ready than ever to play it.
